sections.skill: Describe what technical AI roles typically do

questions.prompt: What does a data scientist typically do?

choices.text: Builds the physical computer chips that every AI model needs in order to run at all
Collects, cleans and analyzes data to answer questions

questions.correct_answer: Collects, cleans and analyzes data to answer questions
questions.intro: Several technical roles work with AI; titles vary by employer. A DATA SCIENTIST collects, cleans and analyzes data to answer questions, often using statistics and programming. A MACHINE LEARNING (ML) ENGINEER builds, trains and runs models so they work reliably in real products. An AI ENGINEER often builds applications on top of existing models, connecting them to data and tools and testing how they behave. All three usually need programming, careful testing and clear communication. Pay and credential requirements vary widely by employer and place, so this course does not state them.

sections.skill: Compare AI roles with roles in a restaurant

questions.prompt: The food taster who studies sales is like whom?
questions.correct_answer: A data scientist
questions.intro: In a restaurant, a FOOD TASTER studies what customers like and which dishes sell, then reports findings; that is like a data scientist. The KITCHEN ENGINEER sets up ovens and equipment so food comes out right every time, even on busy nights; that is like an ML engineer. A CHEF who creates new dishes using ready-made ingredients and equipment is like an AI engineer building applications from existing models.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Read job postings and titles carefully

questions.prompt: Why read tasks instead of titles in a posting?

choices.text: Because titles are always false and are written only to attract as many applicants as possible
Titles overlap and differ between employers

questions.correct_answer: Titles overlap and differ between employers
questions.intro: Job titles overlap and change. One company's "data scientist" may do what another calls "analyst" or "ML engineer." Read the TASKS in a job posting rather than the title. Many postings list more skills than any one person has; they describe an ideal, not a minimum. Government sources such as the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook describe typical duties for US occupations, which helps you compare roles more consistently.

questions.prompt: A posting lists 25 skills. What is a reasonable reading?

Every applicant must have all 25 skills at an expert level before they are allowed to apply
